opening: Questions of the form "can it be done?", and why answering them takes two separate arguments.

steps.prompt: A chessboard has 32 black and 32 white squares. Two opposite corners are cut off; both happen to be black. How many black squares are left?
nudges: What colour are the two removed squares?

steps.prompt: A domino covers two neighbouring squares. Can 31 dominoes cover the 62 remaining squares?
options: No: each domino covers one black and one white square, so 31 dominoes need 31 of each
It depends on how they are placed
nudges: What colours does a single domino cover, wherever it is put?
steps.showed: A condition that every tiling must satisfy fails, so no tiling exists. One short argument settles "impossible".

steps.prompt: Now remove one black and one white square instead. The colour count is balanced again. Does that prove the board can be covered?
options: No: passing a test that every solution must pass proves nothing by itself; someone still has to show a covering
Yes: the only obstacle is gone
No: it can never be covered
nudges: You showed "tiling implies balanced colours". Which direction do you need now?
steps.showed: A necessary condition rules things out. To rule things in, you must build the answer. (Here it can always be done, but that needs its own construction.)

steps.prompt: You have unlimited coins worth 3 and 5. Which amounts from 1 to 15 can NOT be paid exactly?
steps.verify: result = [n for n in range(1, 16) if not any((n - 5 * b) % 3 == 0 for b in range(n // 5 + 1))]

steps.prompt: Why is it certain that every amount from 8 upward can be paid, with no further checking?
options: 8, 9 and 10 can be paid, and adding one more 3-coin to those reaches every larger amount
Because large numbers have many divisors
nudges: If $n$ can be paid, what about $n + 3$?
steps.showed: Three consecutive successes plus a step of 3. That is a construction for every amount that passes the test "at least 8".

steps.prompt: Two numbers, 1 and 2. An operation adds 1 to both of them. Can they ever become equal?
nudges: What does one operation do to the difference of the two numbers?

steps.prompt: Three numbers: 1, 2, 3. An operation picks two of them and adds 1 to each. What is the smallest number of operations that makes all three equal?
nudges: Each operation adds 2 to the total. If all three end at the value $k$, what is the total, and which $k$ are possible?
Once you know the target value, how many times must each number be increased?
steps.showed: The total grows by 2 each time, so the final common value must be even: 4. Then 1 needs three increases, 2 needs two, 3 needs one, and three operations deliver exactly that.

steps.prompt: In that last question, which part was the necessary condition and which was the construction?
options: Necessary: the total changes by 2, forcing the common value to be even. Construction: actually choosing pairs that deliver the required increases
nudges: Which part told you what could not happen, and which part showed something that does happen?
steps.showed: In a contest: guess the condition from small cases, prove it is forced, then find a construction that works whenever it holds.

steps.prompt: A problem asks "for which inputs is it possible?". Which plan answers it completely?
options: Find a condition every possible case must satisfy, and then give a way to build an answer for every input that satisfies it
Find one condition that every possible case satisfies
Build an answer for a few inputs and extrapolate
nudges: What is still unknown if you have done only one of the two halves?
steps.showed: Two halves, and neither can be skipped.

steps.prompt: Prove that every whole number $n \ge 8$ can be written as $3a + 5b$ with whole numbers $a, b \ge 0$.
claims: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 + 3 + 3 and 10 = 5 + 5 can be written this way.
If n can be written this way then so can n + 3, by increasing a by one.
Every n >= 8 is 8, 9 or 10 plus a non-negative multiple of 3 (according to its remainder mod 3), so it can be written this way.
nudges: Which few cases would you check by hand?
How do you get from an amount that works to a larger one?
Why do your hand-checked cases and that step together reach every $n \ge 8$?
steps.showed: Three base cases and a step of 3.

steps.prompt: For which n from 1 to 9 can the numbers 1..n be written in a row p_1, ..., p_n so that the n differences |p_i - i| are all different?
steps.verify:
import itertools
result = [n for n in range(1, 10) if any(len({abs(p[i] - i - 1) for i in range(n)}) == n for p in itertools.permutations(range(1, n + 1)))]
nudges: The differences are n different numbers between 0 and n - 1. What must they add up to?
What is the parity of the sum of all |p_i - i|, whatever the arrangement?
steps.showed: The differences must be 0, 1, ..., n-1, with sum n(n-1)/2. But the sum of |p_i - i| is always even (it has the parity of the sum of p_i - i, which is 0). So n(n-1)/2 must be even: n is 0 or 1 mod 4. Constructions exist for all of those.

steps.prompt: With coins worth 6, 10 and 15, what is the largest amount that cannot be paid exactly?
nudges: No two of the coins are coprime, yet all three together are. Which amounts are payable in each remainder class mod 6?
steps.showed: Work mod 6: the smallest payable amount in each class is 0, 25, 20, 15, 10, 35 (classes 0 to 5), built from 10s and 15s. The worst is 35, so 29 is the last unpayable amount.

steps.prompt: Ten lamps are off. A move switches exactly three lamps of your choice. What is the smallest number of moves that turns all ten on?
nudges: What does a move do to the parity of the number of lit lamps?
The parity rules out some numbers of moves. Is the smallest remaining number actually achievable?
steps.showed: Each move changes the parity, so the number of moves is even; two moves switch at most six lamps. Four moves make twelve switches: nine lamps once and one lamp three times.

reveal.name: Necessary, then sufficient
reveal.statement: To decide for which inputs something is possible: (1) find a condition that every solvable input must satisfy, usually an invariant or a count; (2) show how to construct a solution for every input satisfying it.
reveal.remark: Small cases suggest the condition. If your condition is necessary but you cannot construct, it is probably too weak: brute-force small inputs and compare.
